output.impression: 1. Severe verbal memory impairment: RAVLT immediate recall 28/75 and delayed recall 2/15, a storage-type pattern. 2. Mildly impaired naming (Boston Naming Test 48/60) and semantic fluency (11 animals per minute) and borderline-low letter fluency (FAS 32). 3. Mildly slowed processing speed (Trail Making A 52 s) and impaired set-shifting (Trail Making B 168 s); clock drawing 8/10. 4. Mood screen within normal limits (GDS 5/15). Screening MMSE 24/30, MoCA 21/30. Multi-domain cognitive impairment with amnestic predominance, at a level consistent with mild dementia given the reported functional decline.

output.interpretation: Normal opening pressure, cell count, protein and glucose. Decreased Abeta42 and Abeta42/40 ratio with elevated p-tau181 and total tau: a CSF profile consistent with Alzheimer disease pathology. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions: Donepezil + Zolpidem: no pharmacokinetic interaction; zolpidem itself impairs memory and causes confusion on waking and falls in older adults, independent of donepezil.
Donepezil + Amlodipine: no significant interaction; amlodipine does not slow the heart rate.
Donepezil + Aspirin: cholinesterase inhibitors increase gastric acid secretion, which may add to the gastrointestinal bleeding risk of aspirin; watch for dyspepsia or melaena.
Donepezil + Metformin or atorvastatin: no significant interaction; both add to gastrointestinal upset at initiation.
warnings: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia, heart block and syncope; check pulse before starting and after dose increases (heart rate 74 bpm at this visit) and ask about syncope and conduction disease.

Nausea, diarrhoea, anorexia, weight loss and vivid dreams are common at initiation; start at 5 mg and increase to 10 mg after 4 to 6 weeks if tolerated, and take it in the morning if sleep is disturbed.
Avoid adding anticholinergic medicines, which oppose the effect of cholinesterase inhibitors.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with delayed recall 0/5 not helped by cues, informant-confirmed decline over fourteen months, and loss of instrumental independence (finances taken over, reminders for medicines, lost while driving)
action_criteria.label: Perform a structured cognitive assessment with informant history, a per-domain profile and an explicit account of daily function
action_criteria.rationale: His wife's account decides the stage: she has taken over the finances, he needs reminders and he gets lost while driving [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe storage-type verbal memory impairment with mild naming, semantic fluency, processing speed and set-shifting deficits
action_criteria.label: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the profile and set a baseline
action_criteria.rationale: A storage-type amnestic profile points to Alzheimer disease, whereas a hypnotic, sleep apnoea or small vessel disease mainly slow processing and retrieval [NIA_AA_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No reversible cause: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 (subclinical hypothyroidism), HbA1c 6.9%
action_criteria.label: Order the cognitive laboratory panel to identify reversible or contributing causes
action_criteria.rationale: Thyroid, B12, folate, syphilis and HIV must be checked, and diabetic control measured [AAN_dementia_2018].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Hippocampal atrophy (MTA 1-2, volumes at the 7th and 12th percentiles) with Fazekas grade 2 white matter disease and an incidental arachnoid cyst
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI with a dementia protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and small vessel disease and exclude a mass
action_criteria.rationale: MRI shows the hippocampal atrophy that supports a neurodegenerative cause and the small vessel burden expected with diabetes, hypertension and past smoking [STRIVE_2013].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Amyloid positivity: decreased CSF Abeta42/40 ratio with raised p-tau181, or a positive amyloid PET
action_criteria.label: Establish amyloid status with CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET when the result would change management
action_criteria.rationale: At 62, with small vessel disease and low-light visual misperceptions, amyloid status separates Alzheimer disease from vascular and Lewy body causes and decides eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment; one conclusive test is enough [NIA_AA_2018] [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2
action_criteria.label: Consider an early-onset Alzheimer gene panel only with pre-test genetic counselling; APOE genotype is not a diagnostic test
action_criteria.rationale: Onset at 61 permits testing, but with no family history of early dementia the yield is low and the result informs his children rather than his diagnosis [ACMG_NSGC_2011].

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pharmacokinetic interaction; additive gastrointestinal risk with aspirin; zolpidem is a cognitive risk in its own right
action_criteria.label: Check interactions before starting donepezil
action_criteria.rationale: Before a cholinesterase inhibitor his aspirin, amlodipine, metformin, atorvastatin and zolpidem should be reviewed, with attention to pulse [NICE_NG97].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the decline to subclinical hypothyroidism or defer the dementia diagnosis until the TSH normalizes
Do not attribute the decline to zolpidem or sleep apnoea alone without completing the dementia evaluation
Do not prescribe an antipsychotic for the low-light visual misperceptions, given the risk of severe sensitivity if Lewy body pathology is present [DLB_2017]
Do not start memantine at the mild dementia stage; it is indicated for moderate or severe Alzheimer dementia [NICE_NG97]
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Disclose the diagnosis of early-onset mild Alzheimer dementia to him and his wife, and plan durable power of attorney, advance directives and support for a young-onset diagnosis
Advise him to stop driving until a formal driving assessment, since he has got lost twice on familiar routes
Address safety at home: his wife keeps the finances, medicines in a supervised blister pack, and support for the carer

Deprescribe zolpidem, tapering if he has been taking it most nights, and treat insomnia with sleep hygiene or CBT-I and a check of CPAP adherence; Z-drugs impair memory and cause confusion and falls in older adults [Beers_2023]

Offer amyloid biomarker testing (CSF or amyloid PET) if a biological diagnosis would change management, such as eligibility for anti-amyloid treatment or diagnostic uncertainty; one conclusive test is sufficient [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET].
Offer a trial of a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine or galantamine) for mild Alzheimer dementia after checking pulse, conduction history and current medicines [NICE_NG97].
Repeat TSH and free T4 with TPO antibodies in 2 to 3 months rather than starting levothyroxine; a TSH of 5.8 mIU/L with normal free T4 does not explain the cognitive decline [ETA_SCH_2013].
Manage vascular risk: blood pressure 142/88 mmHg on amlodipine to target, continue the statin, and keep diabetic control (HbA1c 6.9%)

Ask at follow-up about dream enactment, fluctuations and well-formed hallucinations, and examine for parkinsonism, because of the low-light visual misperceptions and the family history of Parkinson disease

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography has no role; he has no cardiac symptoms, murmur or embolic event
He has no palpitations, syncope or falls, so cardiac monitoring is not indicated
Head CT adds nothing when MRI is available and cannot assess hippocampal volume as well

accepted: Early-onset Alzheimer disease (mild dementia, amnestic) with cerebrovascular copathology

differential.key_features: Raised by fleeting peripheral shapes in low light, confusion on waking, mildly slow rapid alternating movements and an uncle with Parkinson disease. Against it: the shapes are recognized misperceptions rather than well-formed hallucinations, waking confusion is explained by zolpidem and sleep apnoea, there is no dream enactment, fluctuation or parkinsonism, and the profile is storage-type with hippocampal atrophy and an Alzheimer CSF profile. Lewy copathology is possible and is reassessed at follow-up

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment as the sole cause
differential.key_features: Fazekas 2 small vessel disease with diabetes, hypertension and past smoking is a real copathology and may add to the slowed processing, but the course is gradual rather than stepwise and the storage-type memory deficit with hippocampal atrophy and the Alzheimer CSF profile show Alzheimer disease as the primary cause
Apathy and withdrawal are present, but there is no disinhibition, compulsion or dietary change, language is fluent with only word-finding pauses, and memory is disproportionately affected
Zolpidem and sleep apnoea (on CPAP) can cause morning confusion and poor attention, but not a progressive fourteen-month storage-type amnesia with loss of financial competence
Apathy and withdrawal, but he denies low mood, GDS is 5/15, and recall is not helped by cues

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic or endocrine cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism; B12, folate, RPR and HIV are normal

key_clinical_evidence: A spouse taking over the finances after unpaid bills, reminders for medicines and getting lost while driving are a loss of instrumental independence: the stage is mild dementia, not mild cognitive impairment [NIA_AA_2011]
Fleeting shapes in low light that the patient recognizes as misperceptions are not well-formed visual hallucinations and are not a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies [DLB_2017]
Fazekas 2 small vessel disease is a contributing copathology, not an alternative explanation for a storage-type memory deficit with an Alzheimer CSF profile [STRIVE_2013]
One conclusive amyloid biomarker test (CSF Abeta42/40 with p-tau, or amyloid PET) is enough [Appropriate_Use_Amyloid_PET]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Subclinical hypothyroidism is rechecked and treated on its own merits, but it does not cause a progressive storage-type amnesia with hippocampal atrophy and an Alzheimer CSF profile
red_herrings.data_point: TSH 5.8 mIU/L with a normal free T4
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the cognitive symptoms to hypothyroidism and defer further dementia workup until thyroid normalization

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Recognized low-light misperceptions and waking confusion on zolpidem with sleep apnoea are not core Lewy body features; without dream enactment, fluctuations or parkinsonism they do not outweigh the amnestic profile and the Alzheimer biomarkers, but they warrant follow-up
red_herrings.data_point: Fleeting shapes in the peripheral vision in low light, confusion on waking, and an uncle with Parkinson disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose dementia with Lewy bodies, or treat the misperceptions with an antipsychotic

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural imaging comes before lumbar puncture to exclude a mass lesion.
Amyloid biomarkers are interpreted against an established clinical syndrome; they are not a screening test.
Genetic testing follows the characterization of the syndrome and pre-test counselling.

findings.result: Alert; oriented to person, place, month and year but not to the date.

MoCA 21/30: visuospatial/executive 2/5 (trail-making, cube copy, clock hands), delayed recall 0/5 with no benefit from category cues, orientation 5/6; naming, attention, language and abstraction without point loss. Serial sevens slow with one error; occasional word-finding pauses.

His wife reports fourteen months of progressive forgetfulness, with the same question repeated three or four times in an hour, and word-finding pauses. He has become withdrawn and apathetic over six months and has given up woodworking and reading; he denies low mood.

Fleeting shapes in the peripheral vision in low light, which he recognizes as misperceptions; confusion on waking from disrupted sleep while taking zolpidem as needed. No dream enactment, tremor or falls reported.

About six months ago his wife found unpaid bills and a significant error in the checking account and has taken over the finances. He needs reminders for medicines and appointments and has got lost twice on familiar driving routes. Basic activities of daily living are independent.

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 21/30, with impairment in delayed recall, visuospatial/executive function and orientation to date. Delayed recall 0/5, with no benefit from category cues. His wife reports fourteen months of progressive memory decline. Instrumental independence is lost: she has taken over the household finances after unpaid bills and an accounting error, he needs reminders for medicines and appointments, and he has got lost while driving. The syndrome therefore meets the functional threshold for mild dementia.

patient.history_present_illness: A 62-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer presents to the neurology outpatient clinic with a one-year history of progressive memory difficulties, brought in by his wife who has been increasingly concerned about his cognitive function. The patient initially noticed difficulty remembering the names of colleagues at professional gatherings approximately 14 months ago, which he attributed to normal aging and retirement-related disengagement. Over the following months, his wife observed that he began repeating questions within the same conversation, sometimes asking the same thing three or four times in an hour. He has had increasing difficulty managing the household finances, which he had always handled independently, and his wife discovered several unpaid bills and a significant accounting error in their checking account about six months ago. She has since taken over financial management. The patient reports intermittent episodes of visual misperceptions, particularly in low-light conditions, where he describes seeing fleeting shapes in his peripheral vision that he initially dismissed as shadows. He has gotten lost twice on familiar driving routes over the past three months, once requiring his wife to guide him home by phone. He occasionally has difficulty finding words during conversation, substituting with vague terms or pausing mid-sentence. He can still perform basic activities of daily living independently, including dressing, grooming, and eating, but his wife notes he now needs reminders for medications and appointments. His sleep has been disrupted, with frequent nocturnal awakenings and occasional confusion upon waking. He has been using zolpidem intermittently for the past several months. The patient denies any headaches, seizures, focal weakness, numbness, or gait disturbance. He denies depressed mood but his wife reports he has become more withdrawn and apathetic over the past six months, spending most of the day watching television rather than pursuing his former hobbies of woodworking and reading. There has been no recent illness, fever, weight loss, or urinary symptoms.

neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No myoclonus. No primitive reflexes (grasp, snout, palmomental). Anosmia not formally tested.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing intact bilaterally without dysmetria. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow bilaterally.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation and strength symmetric. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength normal. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal gait, tandem walk intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; oriented to month and year but not the exact date. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 21/30: visuospatial/executive 2/5 (trail-making error, cube copy error, clock hands misplaced), delayed recall 0/5 (none recovered with category cues), orientation 5/6 (date); abstraction 2/2. Clock drawing mildly disorganized with incorrect hand placement. Serial 7s performed slowly with one error. Conversational speech fluent but with occasional word-finding pauses.
neurological_exam.motor: Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. Muscle bulk and tone normal throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles tendons bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in all extremities. Cortical sensory function intact (graphesthesia, stereognosis).
